slides.title: No secrets in the bundle
slides.summary: Anything shipped to the browser is public: API keys, internal URLs, feature flags and comments.
body: Build tools inline environment variables into JavaScript. If a value is in the bundle, it's public.

ul: Publishable keys only: keys designed to be public (a Stripe publishable key, a maps key restricted by referrer) are fine.
Secret keys stay on a server: call the API through your backend, which adds the key. This includes LLM API keys.
Source maps expose your original code. Upload them to your error tracker instead of serving them publicly, if that matters to you.
Hidden UI isn't access control: hiding an admin button doesn't stop someone calling the admin API.

body: <mark>If the browser can read a value, so can the user and any script on the page.</mark>

body.note: Vite exposes only VITE_-prefixed variables and Next.js only NEXT_PUBLIC_ ones, but anything you import into client code ships. Run a secret scanner (e.g. gitleaks) on the built output in CI.

cells.text: Yes, but assume users can flip them
Mirror them for UX; enforce on the server

figure.alt: Two designs. Wrong: the browser bundle contains a secret API key, sk-live-…, and calls the third-party API directly; anyone can open DevTools, copy the key and use it for their own requests, running up your bill or reading your data. Right: the browser calls your own endpoint /api/summary with its session cookie; your server checks the user is allowed, applies rate limits, adds the secret key from an environment variable and calls the third-party API. The key never leaves the server.

slides.title: Where to keep auth tokens
slides.summary: localStorage is readable by any XSS. HttpOnly cookies aren't, but need CSRF protection.
body: Every storage option trades XSS exposure against CSRF exposure.

ul: localStorage / sessionStorage: easy, but any script on the page can read the token and send it anywhere.
In memory: gone on reload; XSS can still use it while the page is open, but can't easily take it away for later.
HttpOnly cookie: JavaScript can't read it at all. The browser sends it automatically, so you must defend against CSRF.

body: <mark>Prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies for sessions, and keep any tokens short-lived.</mark>

body.text: Set-Cookie: __Host-session=…; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/. The __Host- prefix forces Secure, Path=/ and no Domain, so a subdomain can't overwrite it. Use SameSite=Strict where cross-site links don't need to arrive logged in.

Safari and Firefox block or partition third-party cookies by default. Chrome dropped its plan to remove them (2025), but users can block them. For an embedded widget that needs its own state, use partitioned cookies (CHIPS, the Partitioned attribute), which are keyed to the top-level site.

slides.title: Choosing client storage
slides.summary: Pick storage by size, lifetime and exposure. Anything JavaScript can read, an XSS bug can read too.
body: Browsers offer several stores, each with different limits and risks:

ul: Cookies are small and sent with requests: right for a session ID (HttpOnly), wrong for app data.
localStorage / sessionStorage are synchronous key-value strings, about 5 MB per origin. Fine for preferences like theme or a draft; not for tokens or personal data.
IndexedDB holds large, structured data asynchronously, for offline apps and caches. Its quota is a share of free disk space.
Cache Storage holds HTTP responses for service workers.
Writes beyond the quota throw QuotaExceededError; catch it rather than losing data silently.
navigator.storage.estimate() reports usage and quota; navigator.storage.persist() asks the browser not to evict your data.
Large synchronous localStorage reads block the main thread on every page load.

body: <mark>Store the minimum, for the shortest time, in the least exposed place. Clear it on logout.</mark>
code: // Check space before caching 200 MB of offline maps
const persisted = await navigator.storage.persist(); // ask: don't evict

figure.alt: Five storage options compared. Cookies: about 4 KB each, lifetime set by Expires or Max-Age, readable by JavaScript unless HttpOnly, and sent to the server with every matching request. localStorage: about 5 MB per origin, kept until cleared, readable by any script on the page, never sent automatically. sessionStorage: about 5 MB, cleared when the tab closes, readable by scripts. IndexedDB: large, a share of free disk space, kept until cleared or evicted under storage pressure unless persistence is granted, readable by scripts, asynchronous and structured. Cache Storage: also quota-based, used by service workers for HTTP responses. The rule: anything a script can read, an XSS bug can read. Sessions belong in HttpOnly cookies.

slides.title: Expiry, integrity and sessions done right
slides.summary: Expiry and integrity must be enforced by the server. Client-side timers, encryption and checksums are conveniences, not security.

body.h: Common advice that doesn't hold up

ul: “Encrypt data before putting it in localStorage.” The key has to be in your JavaScript too, so XSS can decrypt it. Don't store the secret at all. If you must keep a key client-side, a non-extractable WebCrypto key in IndexedDB at least stops it being copied out.
“Delete the token with setTimeout when it expires.” An attacker who copied it keeps using it. Expiry must be checked by the server: a short exp claim on JWTs, or a server-side session timeout.

“Store a checksum next to the data to detect tampering.” Anyone who can change the data can recompute the checksum. Integrity needs a secret the client doesn't have: an HMAC or signature verified by the server.
“Set HttpOnly from JavaScript.” Browsers ignore HttpOnly in document.cookie; only the server's Set-Cookie header can set it.

body.h: What good session management looks like

ul: Short-lived access (minutes), with an idle timeout and an absolute timeout on sessions.
Logout destroys the session on the server, not just in the browser.
Re-authenticate before sensitive actions (change email, payout details).
Multi-factor authentication, ideally passkeys (WebAuthn), which can't be phished like passwords and codes.

body: <mark>If the security check runs in the browser, an attacker can skip it. Expiry, integrity and permissions are server jobs.</mark>
code: // Server: session cookie the browser can't read or send cross-site
httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: '/',
maxAge: 30 * 60 * 1000,          // 30 min idle timeout, renewed on use
// Server: integrity with a secret the client never sees

slides.title: OAuth in single-page apps
slides.summary: Use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE, ideally through a backend-for-frontend so tokens never reach JavaScript.
body: RFC 10017 (OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications, August 2026) is the current best practice. It describes three architectures, from most to least secure:

ul: Backend-for-frontend (BFF): a server on your origin runs OAuth and keeps all tokens; the browser only has a session cookie.
Token-mediating backend: the backend gets tokens and hands access tokens to the browser.
Browser-only client: the SPA does OAuth itself with PKCE; tokens live in JavaScript, exposed to any XSS.
Never use the implicit flow (tokens in the URL); RFC 9700 deprecates it.
Always use PKCE and check the state parameter.
Keep access tokens short-lived and use refresh token rotation.

body: <mark>If an XSS bug can read your tokens, it can use them from anywhere. A BFF keeps them out of reach.</mark>

steps.caption: The app makes a one-time secret and sends only its hash.
The user signs in with the identity provider.
A short-lived code comes back, not a token.
Only the holder of the verifier can turn the code into tokens.

figure.alt: Four parties. The browser holds only an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite session cookie: no access or refresh tokens, so XSS cannot steal them. The BFF is a small server on the app's own origin; it runs the OAuth authorization code flow with PKCE as a confidential client, stores the access and refresh tokens server-side, and proxies API calls, attaching the access token. The identity provider issues the tokens to the BFF. The resource API receives requests with a Bearer token from the BFF only.
